title: Should Lecturers Know How Learning Works?
author: Jonathan Firth
summary: Jonathan Firth examines a 2012 paper by Steiner and Hakala arguing that Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) practitioners do not need fluency in the science of learning, only the ability to be 'good consumers' of research. Firth pushes back, arguing that consuming research critically requires foundational knowledge, and that a skills-over-knowledge framing leaves educators vulnerable to acting on misconceptions and learning myths that pervade even the published literature. He acknowledges the pragmatic constraint that most educators cannot become full experts, but argues for a middle path: the level of a 'well-informed generalist' who can recognize key pitfalls, engage critically with research, and take part in scholarly debates about local application. This level is both attainable for busy practitioners and essential for avoiding discredited fads that waste professional development time and harm student outcomes.
points: Steiner and Hakala's position that SoTL practitioners need only be 'good consumers' of research implies educators can figure things out by intuition, which Firth reads as a skills-over-knowledge argument.
Research confirms that many university instructors hold active misconceptions about learning, and that learning myths are widespread in the very literature they encounter.
Firth proposes a pragmatic middle path, the 'well-informed generalist', realistic for busy educators yet sufficient to recognize key pitfalls without full expertise.
Foundational knowledge lets educators engage as genuinely critical consumers of research rather than passive recipients.
Without baseline learning-science knowledge, educators risk investing time in discredited fads and missing the line between evidence-based practice and pedagogical mythology.
quotes: I am not convinced by the argument that educators can be consumers of research without knowledge. This implies that they can figure things out as they go along, using their intuition. It's a skills-over-knowledge argument.
There is a value in knowing enough that you recognise your own errors and have an awareness of key pitfalls.
We know from other research that many university instructors have misconceptions about learning, and that learning myths are widespread in published research to which they may be exposed.
it's feasible to become at least a well-informed generalist, if not an expert. Doing so will help them to engage as critical consumers of research literature.
These faculty, however, are often not experts in the field of learning, and, pressed for time, may rely on strategies that contradict recent research on teaching and learning.
